extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques (discrete math/intro to proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Writing and checking proofs that use (and variations of) mathematical induction, including choice of base case, induction step, handling existentials, proofs on combinatorial/structural objects, and proofs about recursively defined functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by mathematical induction structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a two-part structure: prove a base case P(b) (for some appropriate b) and then prove the induction step 'for arbitrary n assume P(n) and prove P(n+1)'. The text: 'let n be an arbitrary natural number, assuming P(n) is true, and then proving that P(n + 1) is true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the base case and the induction step. In the induction step declare n arbitrary, state the inductive hypothesis (assume P(n)), and show how to derive P(n+1). The inductive hypothesis is often called the inductive hypothesis and is used to relate P(n) to P(n+1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an appropriate base case
rubrics_metrics.description: The base case need not be n = 0; pick the smallest n for which the statement is meant to hold (e.g., n = 5 in the 2^n vs n^2 example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the base case by direct computation or reasoning. If the claim is only for n > m, take n = m as the base. Failing to check the correct base case (or choosing n=0 when the claim doesn't hold there) invalidates the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and use the inductive hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: When carrying out the induction step, clearly state the inductive hypothesis (assume P(n) holds) and show how it helps derive P(n+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out algebraic or logical relationships that let you replace occurrences of P(n)-type expressions with whatever the hypothesis guarantees. Be explicit about where the hypothesis is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate P(n) to P(n+1) algebraically/structurally
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a direct algebraic or structural relationship between the statement for n and the statement for n+1 (e.g., expand (n+1)^2 or use 2^{n+1} = 2*2^n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate the goal and/or the inductive hypothesis (expand, factor, multiply both sides, compare terms) to reduce P(n+1) to a consequence of P(n) plus additional easily-checked inequalities or identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle existential quantifiers by introducing witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: When the inductive hypothesis gives an existential (e.g., 'there exists k such that 3k = n^3 - n'), explicitly introduce a witness variable (k) and construct a new witness (j) for the n+1 case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the textbook technique: use the given existential to 'let k be an integer such that ...' then algebraically produce j (often an expression in k and n) satisfying the needed relation for n+1. You may omit mentioning the final witness name in the polished proof once its construction is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate non-numerical problems into an induction-on-n form
rubrics_metrics.description: Rephrase combinatorial/structural statements in the form 'for every n, every object of size n has property P' (e.g., 'every finite nonempty set B ⊂ A with n elements has a minimal element').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the natural parameter n (number of elements, size, number of chords, etc.) and perform induction on that parameter. Carefully justify that decreasing the parameter (e.g., removing one element) yields an instance where inductive hypothesis applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce to a smaller instance (remove an element / partition)
rubrics_metrics.description: To use the inductive hypothesis on finite sets or tiling problems, produce a smaller sub-instance (e.g., remove one element from a set, split a grid into subgrids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the element or partition strategically (e.g., remove any element b and consider B\{b}, or split a 2^{n+1}×2^{n+1} board into four 2^n×2^n boards) so that the inductive hypothesis applies to the smaller pieces. Provide additional construction (like placing a central tile) that allows the smaller pieces to meet the hypothesis' conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by cases inside the induction step when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inductive argument depends on a dichotomy (e.g., bRc or not bRc), split the induction step into cases and prove P(n+1) in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the cases clearly and apply appropriate reasoning in each. The partial order minimal-element example demonstrates using cases bRc and ¬bRc and different arguments to produce a minimal element in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by contradiction for negative statements
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving a negative property (e.g., 'x is minimal' meaning there is no smaller distinct element), it is often effective to assume the negation and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In both cases of the partial-order example, the text uses contradiction: assume an alleged minimal element is not minimal, find a counterexample, and use antisymmetry/transitivity to contradict uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform scratch work and test small cases first
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing the formal proof, compute initial values, make tables, and experiment to detect patterns or the right choice of base case (examples: table comparing n^2 and 2^n, computing first terms of a recurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scratch work to guess formulas (e.g., sequence looks like 2^n - 1), check base cases, and plan how to relate P(n) to P(n+1). The textbook emphasizes this practice under 'Scratch work' sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recursive definitions and prove properties by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function or sequence is defined recursively, prove properties of it by induction aligned with the recursive definition (e.g., factorial, exponentiation, recursively defined sums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the recursive step (e.g., (n+1)! = (n+1)n!) to relate P(n) to P(n+1). Often the recursive definition gives the exact algebraic step needed in the inductive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and name variables carefully (arbitrary vs existential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between 'let n be arbitrary' (universal quantifier) and 'let k be such that ...' (existential witness) and name them explicitly in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make quantifier structure explicit at the start of the induction step. Avoid the error of treating a variable chosen under an existential as if it demonstrated universality, and avoid using the phrase 'since n was arbitrary then ...' incorrectly (see exercises with incorrect proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware improper use of 'arbitrary' to claim universality mid-proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conclude that because you chose n arbitrarily in the induction step you have already proved the property for all n; the inductive structure must be respected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The incorrect proofs in the exercises illustrate the fallacy: choosing an arbitrary n and assuming n∈A then claiming 'since n was arbitrary, every natural number is an element of A' is invalid. The base case and induction step together yield universality only when correctly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle inequalities by appropriate algebraic manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving inequalities by induction, manipulate both sides (multiply, expand, bound terms) to make the inductive hypothesis applicable (e.g., multiply 2^n > n^2 by 2 to get 2^{n+1} > 2 n^2 and then compare 2 n^2 to (n+1)^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known bounds (like n^2 > 5n for n>5) to bridge gaps. Show each algebraic implication clearly and justify steps that rely on numeric bounds or monotonicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use central constructions to connect subproblems in tiling/partition proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: For tiling arguments on power-of-two boards, place a small configuration (e.g., one L-tromino) that creates solvable subproblems each conforming to the inductive hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the central placement reduces the remaining region to several smaller regions each missing one square; then apply the inductive hypothesis on each sub-region. Include diagrams or clear descriptions of the placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove auxiliary claims or lemmas needed to apply induction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the induction step requires facts about sub-relations or structures (e.g., R' is a partial order or T is a total order), either prove these as auxiliary steps or reference exercises that establish them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State and, if necessary, prove the side claims (like closure properties when restricting relations to subsets) so that the inductive hypothesis legitimately applies to the reduced instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: When strengthening your induction target helps, prove the stronger claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If the desired inequality P(n) is awkward to prove directly, prove a stronger statement Q(n) (e.g., (1+x)^n > 1 + n x) which implies P(n) and whose inductive step is easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a stronger but still true invariant that makes the algebra of the induction step work smoothly; show Q(0) and Q(n)⇒Q(n+1), then deduce original P(n) from Q(n) (text demonstrates replacing (1+x)^n > nx by (1+x)^n > 1+nx).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induction on the appropriate index (not necessarily the obvious one)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the natural parameter is not the variable explicitly mentioned in the statement; pick the right quantity (e.g., number of chords, number of points on a circle, size of set) to induct on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly argue why the chosen parameter decreases when constructing the smaller instance and why base case(s) cover the minimal values of that parameter.
